title: Claude plays Minecraft!

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is structuring an AI agent (Rocky) that plays Minecraft, covering the agentic workflow loop, tool definitions, orchestration via Bedrock, and Return of Control for client-side action execution. Minecraft serves as a general-purpose proving ground for agent concepts without tying to a specific industry vertical. The project is an open-source demo and prototype demonstrated at a conference, not a production system. The talk assumes familiarity with cloud services and agentic workflow concepts but remains accessible to practitioners. This is a conference presentation with live and recorded demos at the AI Engineer World's Fair. All supporting evidence is directly stated in the transcript with excerpts grounding the classification.

summary:
Derek, a Developer Advocate at AWS, presents Rocky, an AI agent that plays Minecraft, built using Amazon Bedrock and AWS serverless technologies. The talk begins with a level-setting overview of agentic workflow: an agent consumes unstructured inputs like chat, uses one or many tools, leverages an LLM, orchestrates multiple times through the tool-LLM loop, and returns a response. In the Minecraft context, chat comes from the game's built-in chat function, tools are the many game actions available (build, dig, farm, fight), and the agent itself becomes an in-game bot named Rocky, short for Bedrock.

Rocky's demonstrated capabilities include answering questions about weather, jumping, locating and following players, finding and interacting with animals like pigs, and digging holes with specified dimensions. An experimental build feature allows Rocky to construct 3D structures from natural language requests. The build feature uses a specialized system prompt instructing Claude to act as an expert Minecraft builder that outputs valid JSON representing block placements for Mineflayer. Strict rules are enforced (blocks placed adjacent to each other, specific allowed blocks) because without them the model produces nonsense. Rocky successfully builds a double decker couch from a natural language request. Notably, Rocky also exhibited unexpected emergent behavior by digging itself out of a hole without being explicitly asked.

The architecture evolved significantly. Initially using LangChain on Lambda with Amazon SageMaker hosting Cohere LLMs, the team migrated to Agents for Amazon Bedrock, keeping the Minecraft server and Mineflayer bot framework on Amazon ECS. Mineflayer cannot run on Lambda because it requires state management. The current demo runs Minecraft and Mineflayer locally, calling out to Agents for Amazon Bedrock remotely. The agent uses Claude 3 Haiku for speed.

Amazon Bedrock provides a common API facade across multiple model providers including Anthropic, Cohere, and Meta. It offers managed agentic workflow features including prompt creation assistance, multi-task orchestration, chain-of-thought tracing, knowledge bases for RAG, guardrails, and critically, Return of Control, which passes action outputs back to the client. Actions like dig accept parameters (depth, width) inferred by the model from natural language. The project is open source with infrastructure defined in CloudFormation and CDK. Derek concludes by sharing a QR code for session feedback, offering AWS credit codes, and directing attendees to the GitHub repository and AWS booth for questions.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Agentic Workflow Overview
sections.summary: Derek introduces the talk about building an agent to play Minecraft and provides a level-setting overview of agentic workflow: an agent takes unstructured inputs like chat, uses one or many tools, leverages an LLM, orchestrates multiple times, and returns a response.

sections.title: Mapping Agentic Workflow to Minecraft and Rocky Introduction
sections.summary: Explains how agentic workflow maps to Minecraft: chat comes from the game's chat function, tools are game actions (build, dig, farm, fight), and the agent becomes an in-game bot named Rocky (short for Bedrock). Lists tools including jump, move to position, locate player, and others. The demo is open source.

sections.title: Recorded Demo of Rocky at AWS Booth
sections.summary: Shows a recording of Rocky demonstrating capabilities: answering weather questions, jumping, finding the player, locating and going to a pig, hitting the pig, digging a 2x2 hole with parameters, and unexpectedly digging out of the hole. Presenter notes human fascination with hitting the pig.

sections.title: Architecture Evolution and Serverless Constraints
sections.summary: Details architecture evolution: started with Minecraft and Mineflayer in a container, LangChain on Lambda, SageMaker hosting Cohere LLMs. Migrated to Agents for Amazon Bedrock with Minecraft/Mineflayer on Amazon ECS. Mineflayer cannot run on Lambda due to state requirements. Current demo runs locally calling out to Bedrock.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock Overview and Agent Configuration
sections.summary: Overview of Amazon Bedrock as a model facade supporting multiple providers. Uses Claude 3 Haiku for speed. Features include Agents, Knowledge bases for RAG, guardrails, prompt creation, orchestration, chain-of-thought tracing, and Return of Control. Console walkthrough shows agent definition, system prompt, and action parameters.

sections.title: Live Demo: Rocky in Minecraft
sections.summary: Live demo begins with display setup issues. Rocky spawns in game, time set to noon. Tests include 'come here' command (successful), dig a small hole (successful), and experimental build feature requesting a double decker couch. Source code shown on screen.

sections.title: Build Feature Deep Dive and Conclusion
sections.summary: The live demo continues with Rocky building a double decker couch. The build feature uses a specialized system prompt instructing Claude to act as an expert Minecraft builder outputting valid JSON for Mineflayer block placement. Strict rules enforce adjacent block placement and restrict allowed blocks; without these rules the model produces nonsense. Rocky successfully builds the couch and Derek sits on it. Derek concludes by sharing a QR code for session feedback, offering AWS credit codes, and directing attendees to the GitHub repo and AWS booth.

demonstrations: Recorded demo at AWS booth: Rocky answers weather question, jumps, finds player, finds and hits pig, digs 2x2 hole, digs itself out of hole
Bedrock console walkthrough: agent configuration showing model selection (Claude 3 Haiku), system prompt, action definitions with parameters
Live demo: Rocky spawns in game, responds to 'come here', digs a small hole, experimental build of a double decker couch from natural language
Live demo conclusion: Derek sits on the built couch, shares QR code for feedback and GitHub link
limitations: Mineflayer cannot run on Lambda because it requires state management
Live demo carries inherent risk: presenter notes you should never live demo with kids, animals, and an LLM
Complexity increased significantly with LangChain approach as more actions and tools were added
Without strict rules in the build system prompt, the model produces nonsense structures
